analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers and independent shops legally diagnose and repair their own digital farm equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors and harvesters are locked by software. Under federal copyright law, bypassing those digital locks to fix equipment can be illegal, which pushes repairs to authorized dealers. This bill would change the law so anyone could bypass the locks for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing digital farm equipment, and could make or sell the tools to do it. It was introduced in December 2023, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers gain the right to fix their own tractors, combines, and other digitally controlled equipment, or to use independent mechanics, instead of waiting for authorized dealers and paying dealer labor and parts rates. Faster, cheaper repairs matter most during planting and harvest windows, when days of downtime can mean real crop losses.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds an exception to the copyright anti-circumvention rules so that bypassing a digital lock to diagnose, maintain, or repair digital agricultural equipment is not a violation of law [S2].
It also makes it lawful to build, import, sell, or provide the tools, software, and parts used for those repairs, so independent shops and farmers can actually get what they need to do the work [S2].
The exemption covers 'digital electronic agricultural equipment,' defined broadly as any farm product that depends partly or wholly on attached or embedded electronics to function [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers would lose a revenue stream from dealer-only repairs and licensed diagnostic software, and would lose control over who fixes their machines and at what price. Authorized dealers would face new competition from independent repair shops.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers argue that unrestricted access to equipment software creates safety, emissions-compliance, and cybersecurity risks, since tampering with engine and emissions controls can affect pollution output and machine safety [S2].
The bill is written without conditions, so it applies to any digital farm equipment and any repair purpose; a more tailored version might carve out emissions or safety-critical software [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers, the upside is large: cheaper, faster repairs and less downtime during critical planting and harvest windows. The main cost falls on manufacturers' repair and software revenue, and the bill's blanket wording does raise fair questions about emissions and safety software that a more careful draft could address. On balance, the benefits to equipment owners outweigh the commercial loss to manufacturers, though the lack of any engineering safeguards is a genuine weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the Farm Freedom to Repair Act on December 19, 2023 [S1].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and that was the last action on it [S4].

The bill text would amend federal copyright law to exempt diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of digital agricultural equipment from the prohibitions on circumventing technological protection measures and trafficking in circumvention tools [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers keep their control over the repair market, and farmers keep paying dealer prices and waiting on dealer scheduling for repairs to locked equipment.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; it had no other support in the chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the remainder of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers
against.role: Equipment makers with locked, dealer-serviced machines
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed right-to-repair legislation that would open their machines' software to independent repair.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support is unknown.

industries.note: Manufacturers currently restrict repair of digitally locked equipment to authorized dealers and licensed software, which keeps repair prices and scheduling under their control. The bill would remove that legal lever, cutting into dealer service revenue and unlocking cheaper, faster repairs for farmers.
Dealers would lose a captive service market to independent shops and owner repairs, but could still sell parts and compete for complex work.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and aftermarket tool makers
industries.note: The bill would make it legal to sell diagnostic and repair tools and to service locked farm equipment, opening a market now largely closed to them.
